3d-bowling-176-display--bowl3d-176only.deck: JAMDAT added camera angles and a disco alley to its phone bowling game.

overview.text: A shot starts with four decisions made on timing meters: where to stand, where to aim, how much power to use and how much spin to put on the ball. The 3D edition lets players replay a shot from different angles using the number keys. One of its three alleys has disco lights.

development.text: JAMDAT described Bowling 3D in its annual report as a new edition for high-end phones. Its earlier Bowling 2 already supported playing over the network. GameSpot found that the new game discarded network matches and kept local pass-and-play, despite adding replay and a better sense of being in an actual bowling alley.

release.text: GameSpot reviewed Bowling 3D on the LG VX8000 in February 2005, calling it one of the handset’s launch games. Avery Score liked the replays and the distant sound of other lanes, but thought the omission of online play made the older Bowling 2 a better choice for returning players.

notes.text: The 176-labelled package contains a save filename of jamdatbowling3dsave.dat2. Its executable and four bowling-resource filenames match the ones listed inside the separately preserved JBowling3D package. That links these copies to the JAMDAT title family. Their exact retail device builds remain open.

quotes.text: It’s also possible to view each shot from multiple camera angles, which are chosen by pressing one of the number keys.
quotes.speaker: Avery Score

aliens-vs-predator-3d--avp.deck: Superscape Moscow built a first-person rail shooter around the limits of a phone keypad.

overview.text: The phone moves you through each level while you line up shots. Superscape Moscow used that arcade rail-shooter format for the 3D game, its second adaptation of the film after a 2D platform adventure. The team designed five levels and three modes, with timed and survival play unlocked through the story.

development.text: Gregory Herboek, Superscape Moscow’s creative director, said the team sketched every level and planned enemy placements in a spreadsheet. That let the designers control the difficulty from the opening encounters through the final fight with the Alien Queen. Fox supplied reference material and signed off at each milestone. After the team reached release candidate, it tested against operators’ rules and ported the game to multiple devices.

Herboek said the aiming system was designed to spend less time lining up targets. The build could play two or three sounds together and change the audio in response to the action. Predators carried different weapons, and alien warriors could jump from walls and ceilings.

release.text: In April 2006 Herboek told readers to look in their operator’s game catalog in the United States. MobyGames dates the BREW release to 2006. Superscape later made a separate mobile game based on AvP: Requiem.

notes.text: The package includes avp3d and a bundled iSwerve module. Camera Phone Darts also preserves a module with the same name and version string. The exact retail handset for this AvP package is still unknown.

quotes.text: We wanted to make the game more intense, more action, more about shooting than exploring.
quotes.speaker: Greg Herboek

bioshock-3d--bio3d.deck: Studio Tridev brought Rapture to BREW using its ICE 3D engine.

overview.text: The phone version of BioShock put a first-person Rapture on BREW. IG Fun announced the rights in February 2008, and by that May CEO Sean Malatesta had brought a demonstration to the BREW conference. It ran without player input. Malatesta said the phone was drawing the scene live. A separate 2D edition was in the works for phones that could not run it.

development.text: The 3D credits identify Studio Tridev as developer and Indiagames as distributor. Arjun Nair produced the project, Chaithanya K Singamala led programming and Poornima Seetharaman led game design. At GDC in March 2009, Malatesta described working with phones that could handle just one audio channel and had different graphics capabilities. The team managed to reproduce dynamic lighting in some parts of the 3D build.

Lead designer Poornima Seetharaman recalled that 2K shared the original design document and some art while Studio Tridev rebuilt the game in C/C++. The team switched from Mascot to its own ICE 3D engine to get better performance. She used doors and the direction the player was facing to control when enemies loaded. She also pitched cutting Arcadia to 2K, which signed off on the change.

Engine developer Pradip Bhattacharya recalled that the LG Voyager could use hardware acceleration. For phones without a dedicated graphics processor, the team supplied a software renderer using the phone’s CPU. On the creative side, Nitin Dhamse’s later portfolio and reel show models and animations from the project, including the Breadwinner Splicer and Little Sisters.

Hidden Palace catalogs a level editor and map files from both parts of the project. A May 2009 build documents development of the first part. The separate August 2009 prototype preserves work on Part 2, which the preservation record lists as unreleased.

release.text: The Verizon BREW game arrived in February 2010. MobyGames and Hidden Palace give February 8, while the BioShock Wiki gives February 9. The released adaptation ends at Smuggler’s Hideout. The second part continued the story in levels such as Fort Frolic, which are documented from an unreleased prototype.

crittercrunch--crittercrunch.deck: Capybara’s puzzle game lets Biggs turn a canopy full of critters into one long food chain.

overview.text: Biggs grabs smaller creatures with his tongue and shoots them into the mouths of bigger ones. When a critter gulps down its fill and bursts, matching neighbours can go with it. The game grew from an original mobile project at Toronto’s Capybara Games.

development.text: Lead programmer Radek Koncewicz built the prototype to try out rules and test the limits of the phones. At first, two neighbouring critters would only chain together if they had eaten the same amount of food. Playtesters had trouble keeping track. Koncewicz proposed chaining by colour alone, which made the board easier to read and sped up play.

Koncewicz built two level editors and a Photoshop export script and wrote a guide for outside teams porting the game. Vic Nguyen drew and animated the characters and David Hoang worked on the backgrounds. Kenneth Yeung wrote procedural effects. The studio also built its own tool to automate part of the move from Java to BREW.

release.text: The mobile game won Best Game and Audio Achievement at the first IGF Mobile awards in February 2008. Capy co-founder Nathan Vella said carriers had initially passed it over. Verizon picked it up and featured it after the awards.

notes.text: MobyGames dates BREW to 2007. Vella places Verizon’s pickup after the February 2008 awards. The first day of BREW availability and the team behind this specific build remain unconfirmed. The surviving named credits cover the original mobile production and Java edition.

doodle-jump--ddj.deck: Lima Sky’s game went from pencil sketches to the App Store to Verizon’s BREW catalog.

overview.text: The Doodler bounces automatically. Your job is to guide it onto the next platform and keep climbing as the screen scrolls up.

development.text: Doodle Jump started as Hop, Bunny, Hop!, a sequel to Lima Sky’s Eat, Bunny, Eat! The brothers had an engine but kept getting stuck on the artwork. When they returned to the project, Igor Pusenjak decided the pencil sketches looked better than the graphics they were trying to replace them with.

On the original iPhone game, Igor Pusenjak imagined a black hole throwing you into another player’s game so they could rescue you. Marko Pusenjak suggested drawing a mark where another player fell so you could pass their score while you climbed. Marko said the first version took about two months to develop in Xcode.

release.text: In 2009, Lima Sky agreed to bring Doodle Jump to six more mobile platforms with RealNetworks. MobyGames dates the U.S. BREW release on Verizon to March 16, 2010, a year after the iPhone debut. RealNetworks’ GameHouse label announced a separate Doodle Jump Deluxe for feature phones in June 2011, with four added themes.

development.text: Mobile programmer Jacob Enget worked on DOOM II RPG as part of a six-person team. He puts its multiplatform production at ten months. The low-end engine had a 300 KB memory limit. driv3r--driv3r.deck: Sorrent gave Tanner his own top-down city chases for mobile phones.

overview.text: An undercover cop with a getaway driver’s cover story, Tanner races the clock, rams rivals and can trade a wrecked car for whatever’s passing. The phone adaptation puts its take on the console game’s Miami, Nice and Istanbul under an overhead camera.

development.text: Sorrent’s Jill Braff said the studio would make the phone game in-house and market it alongside Atari’s console release. katamari--katamari.deck: The Prince starts inside a phone, rolling up microchips and transistors before taking his katamari outside.

overview.text: The Prince rolls a ball that picks up anything small enough to stick. Grow it past the size of a dog or a television and those become fair game, too. Rolling with Katamari brings that loop to isometric rooms and neighbourhoods. Its tutorial takes place inside the phone, where the first things to collect are microchips and transistors.

development.text: Keita Takahashi traced the original PlayStation 2 game to a prototype collaboration between Namco and the Digital Hollywood school. Namco’s team handled design, code and art direction. The students made the objects players could roll up. For the Western phone game, Namco Networks advertised 30 levels, including ones made specifically for phones.

release.text: Namco Networks announced Rolling with Katamari for selected North American carriers in November 2008 and planned seasonal downloads on supporting phones. Reviewing the Java edition, Jon Mundy enjoyed the little environments and the King’s dialogue, though he found the steering became touchy as the ball grew.

Japan had more than one keypad version. The 2D Katamari-kun came to Namco EZ Games in November 2007. At Tokyo Game Show in October 2008, KDDI separately showed the 3D Katamari Mobile for au. Directional keys steered and repeated presses of the centre button triggered the Prince Dash. Bandai Namco announced its release for April 30, 2009, through the ¥315-a-month Namco EZ Games service.

orcs-elves-ii--oe2.deck: A thief steals a talking wand to save his village in Fountainhead’s second first-person RPG.

overview.text: Valin needs the wand Ellon to save his village, and Ellon would rather be back with his previous owner. In the first-person, turn-based sequel, you take Valin through dwarven towns, caverns and haunted forests. You can also take control of his pet mouse, Bob, and send him into spaces a thief won’t fit.

development.text: The setting grew out of tabletop adventures John Carmack made for Katherine Anna Kang. By the time of the sequel, the pair had already worked with Fountainhead on DOOM RPG and the first Orcs & Elves. Kang described their working relationship in an October 2007 interview. Carmack would write the engine and spell out what the hardware could handle with the programmers, then Kang developed the design, story and characters within those limits.

Kang was running id Mobile by November 2007. The Java sequel credits name her and Carmack for the original story. They also credit artists Matthew C. Ross and Sarah Sage, with Ross and Rich Douglas sharing music and sound.

release.text: EA announced Orcs & Elves II for phones in July 2007 alongside the Nintendo DS edition of the first game. On December 3 it reported that the sequel was available on most North American carriers, with Europe due in early 2008. The preserved build identifies itself internally as orcsandelves2.

Patrick Gann finished the game in about six hours for RPGFan. His low-end handset struggled with the graphics, but he singled out the additions to the first-person dungeon crawling, including picking locks, breaking out of prison and controlling Bob.

paragraphs.text: On a Verizon phone in 2002, a game download started in a menu called the BREW Shop. Verizon took the service nationwide in June and renamed it Get It Now by September. Get Games sat alongside menus for pictures, ringtones and other applications. The carrier ran the download server and handled the bill.

Qualcomm had announced the Binary Runtime Environment for Wireless the year before as an application environment for CDMA devices. Its developer kit, handset software and distribution system served different parts of the same process. A studio could write a game against Qualcomm’s tools, while a wireless carrier decided how to sell it on the phones it supported.

KDDI and Okinawa Cellular announced their first BREW phone, Toshiba’s A5304T, in January 2003. The commercial service opened on February 21. It gave Japanese publishers a route to au customers on KDDI’s network. A Japanese EZweb listing and a Western review can describe different mobile adaptations of the same series, as the Katamari record shows.

platform.title: Testing before a download could go on sale

paragraphs.text: Summus submitted a text-and-image application to TRUE BREW testing in December 2001. The testing lab, NSTL, sent back a list of items to address. In January the company told shareholders it had made revisions and planned to resubmit, while it evaluated a game for certification. In the same letter the developers were pursuing a separate J2ME port.

When Qualcomm promoted OpenGL ES support on its mobile chipsets in March 2005, Gameloft named Asphalt: Urban GT and Ghost Recon among the games it was developing with the technology. The archive also has OpenGL ES examples and QX samples, whose filenames and contents give a different view of the platform from the retail games.

A Qualcomm conference talk took developers through a 3D test scene called Neocore. The QX toolset included Maya and 3ds Max exporters, a particle editor and a texture optimizer. The talk reports the scene going from 5–10 to 30 frames per second on the test chipset after tuning. Texture compression, mesh layout and the decision to skip objects outside the view were among the steps shown.
